narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2016 Springer Nature book chapter has become a clear reference point in human pose estimation, with 544 OpenAlex citations and top-1% citation standing for its field and year. Its influence is concentrated in computer vision and adjacent machine-learning work, where it continues to be cited as the field moves toward more structured and accurate keypoint and pose models. The record also shows limited but real teaching uptake and open-access circulation.

Full narrative

Human Pose Estimation via Convolutional Part Heatmap Regression, by Adrian Bulat and Georgios Tzimiropoulos, sits at the center of a fast-moving area of computer vision. The citation record indicates substantial scholarly uptake: 544 OpenAlex citations, with percentile standing in the top 1% for its field and year. That level of attention suggests the work has served not just as a paper to be cited, but as a methodological reference point in later pose-estimation research.

The citing landscape shows that its influence is strongest within human pose and action recognition, but it also reaches related areas such as video surveillance and tracking, hand gesture recognition, gait analysis, and broader neural-network applications. Recent citing papers continue to frame the work as part of the technical lineage for pose estimation, including newer studies on real-time 2D pose estimation, low-resolution pose estimation, and graph-structured or multi-scale keypoint modeling. This pattern suggests the chapter’s ideas have remained useful as a basis for refinement rather than being confined to one short-lived research wave.

The work’s reach is international and heavily education-facing. Most citing works come from academic institutions, with additional use in company, government, healthcare, and nonprofit settings. The record also shows an open version in institutional and repository channels, six library holdings, and one YouTube-linked teaching instance that explicitly references the paper in course material. Together, these signals point to a book chapter that is both research-facing and usable as a pedagogical anchor in computer vision and pattern-recognition teaching.

There is also limited evidence of broader societal alignment through the Sustainable Development Goals, specifically Sustainable Cities and Communities. That does not by itself establish direct policy influence, but it does indicate that the work’s techniques are relevant to application domains where human understanding in visual environments matters. Public event data were not available in the supplied record, so the narrative of impact here rests mainly on scholarly citation, disciplinary spread, open availability, and teaching adoption.

Overall, the record shows a durable and influential contribution to pose-estimation research. Its impact is best understood as foundational and cumulative: a technical advance that has continued to inform later work across computer vision, machine learning, and related applied vision tasks.
